title: Git Disaster Recovery Without Panic
description: Thirty-three realistic Git recovery problems. Practice reading reflogs and saving lost commits, including work left on detached HEAD. Learn which undo command fits the situation and how to repair shared history without erasing a teammate's work.

questions.title: You found a possible lost commit at `7ac91e2`. What should you do first?
questions.description: The repository is stable, but you are not sure that `7ac91e2` is the right recovery point.

options.text: Create `rescue/lost-work` at `7ac91e2`, then inspect the commit
Immediately run `git reset --hard 7ac91e2`
Expire every reflog so Git stops changing the evidence
Force-push `7ac91e2` to the shared default branch

questions.explanation: Run `git branch rescue/lost-work 7ac91e2` before changing anything else. The new branch keeps the commit reachable without moving `HEAD` or touching your files. Inspect it with `git show` and compare it with the current branch. A hard reset can discard local work, while a force-push changes shared history before you know what needs fixing.

questions.title: What does a Git reflog primarily record?

options.text: Updates to local refs, including movements recorded in the `HEAD` reflog
Every line ever typed in the terminal
A server-wide audit log automatically shared by every clone
Only commits that remain reachable from a current branch

questions.explanation: A reflog records updates to local refs. The `HEAD` reflog also records branch switches, so it often helps after a reset, rebase, or detached HEAD session. It is not a shell transcript or a shared server log. It can name commits that no current branch reaches.

questions.title: Why can `HEAD@{2}` name a different commit from `HEAD~2`?

images.alt: A commit chain C1 through C4 with a curved green arrow labelled HEAD tilde 2 arcing from C4 back two parent links to land on C2. Beside it, a HEAD reflog table listing HEAD at brace 0 through brace 3: brace 0 is the commit that produced C4, brace 1 is a checkout from topic to main, brace 2 is a commit reached on the topic branch landing on a separate commit X that is not part of the C1 through C4 chain, and brace 3 is the commit that produced C2. HEAD tilde 2 lands on C2; HEAD at brace 2 lands on X.
images.caption: `HEAD~2` always walks two parent links. `HEAD@{2}` is whatever `HEAD` pointed to two ref-updates ago — they can name different commits.

options.text: `HEAD@{2}` means two `HEAD` updates ago, while `HEAD~2` follows two first-parent links
`HEAD@{2}` counts merge parents, while `HEAD~2` counts calendar days
`HEAD@{2}` is always a remote commit, while `HEAD~2` is always local
They are aliases and can never differ

questions.explanation: Reflog ordinals count earlier values of a ref. Commits, resets, rebases, and branch switches can all add entries. `HEAD~2` does something different: it follows the first parent twice through the commit graph. Do not guess a reflog entry from the number of commits in the graph.

questions.title: After your local hard reset, a teammate makes a fresh clone. Can they inspect your old `HEAD@{1}`?

options.text: No. Your reflog belongs to your clone and is not transferred
Yes. Every clone receives every contributor's `HEAD` reflog
Yes, but only after `git fetch --reflogs`
No, because reflogs never record resets

questions.explanation: Reflogs are local to one repository. A fresh clone starts its own reflog and cannot read `HEAD@{1}` from your clone. If only your object database contains the lost commit, recover it there. Another existing clone may also have a copy.

questions.title: How should you recover this clean, private branch after an accidental reset?
questions.description:
The working tree is clean. `git reflog` shows:

```text
91be320 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~2
c3c8a11 HEAD@{1}: commit: finish migration
5bd206a HEAD@{2}: commit: add migration tests
```

options.text: Create `rescue/pre-reset` at `c3c8a11`, inspect it, then reset the branch to `c3c8a11`
`git reset --hard HEAD~2`
`git revert 91be320`
`git rebase --skip`

questions.explanation: The reflog shows that `c3c8a11` was the branch tip just before the reset. First run `git branch rescue/pre-reset c3c8a11` so the commit has a stable name. After you inspect it, `git reset --hard c3c8a11` restores this private branch. Before using `--hard`, also check that no untracked or ignored files are in the way.

questions.title: A deleted branch's commit still appears in a reflog. How do you restore the branch?

options.text: Create a new branch at the recovered commit with `git branch recovered-work <commit>`
Run `git switch -c recovered-work` at the current `HEAD`
Run `git restore --staged <commit>`
Delete the reflog entry so the old branch becomes visible

questions.explanation: Deleting a branch removes its name, but the commit may still exist. If a reflog gives you the commit, run `git branch recovered-work <commit>`. This creates a new ref at the recovered commit. Creating a branch at the current `HEAD` would point to the wrong place, and `git restore --staged` changes the index rather than branch refs.

questions.title: You made a useful commit while `HEAD` was detached, and `HEAD` still points to it. How do you keep it?

options.text: `git switch -c rescue-detached`
`git switch --detach HEAD~1`
`git reset --hard origin/main`
`git branch -D rescue-detached`

questions.explanation: Run `git switch -c rescue-detached` while `HEAD` still points to the commit. Git creates the branch at that commit and switches to it. New commits will advance the branch instead of remaining detached.

questions.title: You already switched away from commits made on a detached `HEAD`. How do you recover them?

options.text: Find the abandoned tip in `git reflog`, inspect it, then create a branch at that commit
Run `git switch -c rescue` and assume the current `HEAD` is the abandoned tip
Run `git pull --force` to download the detached commits
Revert the branch switch commit

questions.explanation: The current `HEAD` no longer points to the abandoned tip, so creating a branch there would save the wrong commit. Find the old tip in the `HEAD` reflog, inspect it, and create a branch at its hash. You cannot revert a branch switch because it is not a commit.

questions.title: Which statements about commit-level `git reset` modes are true?

images.alt: A table comparing three git reset modes across three columns: HEAD (branch), Index (staged), and Working tree. `--soft` moves only HEAD, leaving the index and working tree unchanged. `--mixed`, the default, moves HEAD and resets the index but leaves the working tree unchanged. `--hard` moves HEAD, resets the index, and also resets the working tree, highlighted in red as the only mode that can discard uncommitted edits.
images.caption: Each mode does everything the one above it does, plus more — only `--hard` rewrites files on disk.

options.text: `git reset --soft <commit>` moves the branch tip but leaves both index and working tree unchanged
`git reset --mixed <commit>` moves the branch tip, resets the index, and leaves working-tree files unchanged
`git reset --hard <commit>` resets the branch tip, index, and working tree. It may overwrite untracked files
`git reset --soft <commit>` is the safest way to erase sensitive uncommitted files from disk

questions.explanation: `--soft` moves the branch but leaves the index and working tree alone. `--mixed`, the default, also resets the index. `--hard` goes further and makes the working tree match the target commit, so it can destroy local file changes. `--soft` cannot erase a file because it does not touch the working tree.

questions.title: How do you unstage `config.ts` while keeping its working-tree edits?

options.text: `git restore --staged config.ts`
`git restore --worktree config.ts`
`git reset --hard HEAD -- config.ts`
`git clean -f config.ts`

questions.explanation: With `--staged`, `git restore` copies the version from `HEAD` into the index by default. It does not change the working-tree file, so your edits stay on disk but are no longer staged. `git restore --worktree` would target the file contents you want to keep.

questions.title: How do you restore only `src/parser.ts` from commit `a41d2c0` into the working tree?

options.text: `git restore --source=a41d2c0 --worktree -- src/parser.ts`
`git reset --hard a41d2c0`
`git revert a41d2c0 -- src/parser.ts`
`git rebase --onto src/parser.ts a41d2c0`

questions.explanation: `git restore --source=<tree> --worktree -- <path>` copies one path from the chosen commit into the working tree. It does not move the current branch. A hard reset affects the whole branch, index, and working tree. `git revert` and `git rebase` do not restore one file this way.

questions.title: A bad commit reached a shared, protected branch. How should you normally undo it?

images.alt: Three rows of a commit chain. Before: commits A, B, C, D with main at D and C marked as a bad commit. After git revert C: the same A, B, C, D chain is unchanged, with a new commit E added after D that reverts C, and main now points at E. After git reset --hard B: A and B stay solid with main now pointing at B, while C and D are drawn as dashed, grayed-out circles labelled unreachable from any ref.
images.caption: Revert adds a new commit and keeps history intact, so teammates can pull the correction without repairing their own history.

options.text: Use `git revert <faulty-commit>` and send the new commit through the normal review flow
Remove it locally with `git reset --hard <parent>` and force-push
Delete the branch and recreate it from a local reflog
Run an interactive rebase on every teammate's clone

questions.explanation: `git revert` creates a new commit that reverses the bad commit's effect. Teammates can pull the correction without repairing their local history. Resetting or rebasing the published branch would rewrite commit IDs and force everyone downstream to deal with the rewrite.

questions.title: How do `git revert` and a commit-level `git reset` differ?

images.alt: Three rows of a commit chain. Before: commits A, B, C, D with main at D and C marked as a bad commit. After git revert C: the same A, B, C, D chain is unchanged, with a new commit E added after D that reverts C, and main now points at E. After git reset --hard B: A and B stay solid with main now pointing at B, while C and D are drawn as dashed, grayed-out circles labelled unreachable from any ref.
images.caption: Revert adds a new commit and keeps history intact. Reset moves the branch pointer and can leave commits unreachable.

options.text: Revert adds a commit that reverses an earlier change. Reset moves the current branch tip
Revert moves a branch without a commit; reset always creates an inverse commit
Both commands only modify untracked files
Both commands preserve identical commit IDs and graph shape

questions.explanation: Revert keeps the existing history and adds a new commit with the opposite change. A commit-level reset moves the current branch to another commit. Depending on the reset mode, it may also change the index and working tree. This is why revert is usually safer for shared history, while reset fits unpublished work.

questions.title: Why must you normally choose a mainline parent when reverting a merge?

options.text: Git needs to know which parent is the baseline against which the merge's effect should be reversed
Merge commits have no tree and must borrow one from a parent
The number selects how many later commits should also be reverted
The number identifies a remote repository

questions.explanation: A merge has more than one parent, so Git needs to know which parent is the mainline you want to keep. `git revert -m <parent-number> <merge>` reverses the merge relative to that parent. The choice also affects later merges: Git still treats the reverted merge's ancestors as already merged.
questions.references:
[Git manual: git-revert, `--mainline`](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-revert)

[Git project how-to: Revert a faulty merge](https://git-scm.com/docs/howto/revert-a-faulty-merge)

questions.title: Which commands match the stated goal?

options.text: Use reset to move a private branch tip when rewriting its unpublished history is acceptable
Use revert to record the reversal of an already-shared change
Use rebase to replay selected unpublished commits onto a different base
Use restore to change the ancestry of a published branch

questions.explanation: Reset moves refs. Revert adds a commit that reverses an earlier change. Rebase replays commits and rewrites their history. Restore changes paths in the index or working tree, not commit ancestry. Rewriting a branch that other people use requires coordination and a guarded push.

questions.title: What usually happens to commits that rebase replays onto a new base?

images.alt: Before: a commit graph where main is at C on the chain A, B, C, and topic forked from B with commits X and Y, with topic pointing at Y. After git rebase main while on topic: the main chain A, B, C is unchanged, and topic now points at two new commits X-prime and Y-prime replayed on top of C. The original X and Y are drawn as dashed, grayed-out ghost circles still connected to B, labelled orphaned, same parent B, but no ref reaches them.
images.caption: `X'` and `Y'` are copies of `X` and `Y`'s changes replayed onto the new base — new object IDs, new parents.

options.text: Their changes are replayed and normally become new commit objects with new identities
The original commits are edited in place while keeping their object IDs
Only the branch name changes; commit parent links stay identical
Every rebased commit becomes a merge commit

questions.explanation: Rebase finds the commits to replay, checks out the new base, and applies those changes in order. This is similar to a series of cherry-picks. Because the new commits have different parents, they normally get new object IDs. The reflog may still name the old branch tip until its entries expire.

questions.title: A rebase stopped at a conflict. Which statements are true?

options.text: After resolving and staging conflicts, `git rebase --continue` resumes the rebase
`git rebase --abort` returns to the state from before the rebase
`git rebase --skip` omits the current patch, so it can drop work you meant to keep
`git rebase --continue` automatically chooses the semantically correct conflict resolution

questions.explanation: Resolve the files and stage them before running `git rebase --continue`. Git cannot decide what the code should mean. Use `--abort` to return to the state from before the rebase. Use `--skip` only when you truly want to omit the current patch.

questions.title: How does `git rebase --quit` differ from `git rebase --abort`?

options.text: `--quit` stops managing the rebase but leaves `HEAD`, index, and working tree as they are; `--abort` resets to the original state
`--quit` deletes the branch, while `--abort` deletes only conflicted files
`--quit` publishes the partial rebase, while `--abort` force-pushes the old branch
They are exact aliases

questions.explanation: `--abort` cancels the rebase and returns to the original branch state. `--quit` only removes the rebase's administrative state. It leaves `HEAD`, the index, and the working tree unchanged. If rebase created an autostash, `--quit` saves it in the stash list.

questions.title: Why should `ORIG_HEAD` not be your only bookmark during a complicated recovery?

options.text: Commands such as reset can overwrite it. A rescue branch keeps its own name
`ORIG_HEAD` always points to the repository's root commit
`ORIG_HEAD` exists only on remote servers
`ORIG_HEAD` stores file contents but never a commit

questions.explanation: More than one history-changing command writes `ORIG_HEAD`. For example, `git reset` can replace the value you hoped to recover. Treat `ORIG_HEAD` as a temporary convenience. Once you find an important commit, give it a rescue branch or tag before running more commands.

questions.title: An interactive rebase produced the wrong result. Where should you look for the old branch tip?

images.alt: Before: a commit graph where main is at C on the chain A, B, C, and topic forked from B with commits X and Y, with topic pointing at Y. After git rebase main while on topic: the main chain A, B, C is unchanged, and topic now points at two new commits X-prime and Y-prime replayed on top of C. The original X and Y are drawn as dashed, grayed-out ghost circles still connected to B, labelled orphaned, same parent B, but no ref reaches them.
images.caption: The rebase replays commits onto the new base; the originals stay in place, unreachable from any current ref except the branch's own reflog.

options.text: The branch or `HEAD` reflog, then anchor the candidate tip with a rescue branch
Only the working-tree file modification times
The current branch's first parent, which is guaranteed to be the old tip
The remote default branch, which automatically stores every local pre-rebase tip

questions.explanation: The branch reflog records its earlier tip. Find the pre-rebase commit there, inspect it, and create a rescue branch at that commit. Reflog positions change as you run more commands, so do not leave the commit identified only as something like `@{1}`.
questions.references:
[Git manual: git-rebase, previous branch tip](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase)

[Git manual: git-reflog](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-reflog)

questions.title: After upstream was rewritten, what does `git rebase --onto origin/main origin/main@{1} topic` try to do?
questions.description: Assume `origin/main@{1}` really is the old upstream tip and `topic` contains work based on that old tip.

options.text: Replay the part of `topic` after the old upstream tip onto the new `origin/main`
Reset `origin/main` on the server back to its old tip
Revert every commit currently reachable from `origin/main`
Merge both versions of upstream and preserve duplicate copies of every topic commit

questions.explanation: Git takes the commits reachable from `topic` but not from the old upstream tip, then replays them onto the current `origin/main`. This is Git's documented hard-case recovery pattern. Check that `origin/main@{1}` is really the old tip. A wrong boundary can bring back commits that upstream removed on purpose.
questions.references: [Git manual: git-rebase, recovering from an upstream rebase](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase#_recovering_from_upstream_rebase)

questions.title: After a coordinated rewrite, which push rejects an unexpected update to remote `main`?
questions.description: You agreed that remote `main` may be replaced only if it still points to `a1b2c3d4a1b2c3d4a1b2c3d4a1b2c3d4a1b2c3d4`.

options.text: `git push --force-with-lease=refs/heads/main:a1b2c3d4a1b2c3d4a1b2c3d4a1b2c3d4a1b2c3d4 origin main:main`
`git push --force origin main:main`
`git push origin :main`
`git push --all --force origin`

questions.explanation: The explicit lease says that remote `main` must still point to the expected object ID. Git rejects the push if someone has updated the branch since then. Plain `--force` removes that protection. Deleting `main` or forcing every ref would change more than the team agreed to change.

questions.title: Why is `--force-with-lease` weaker without an expected object ID when tools fetch in the background?

options.text: A background fetch can update the remote-tracking ref used by the lease, even if you never reviewed the new commits
Background fetch rewrites every local commit with a new hash
A lease without an object ID disables authentication for the remote
An explicit expected commit causes Git to ignore all remote changes

questions.explanation: Without an expected value, the lease compares the remote branch with your remote-tracking ref. A background fetch can update that local ref even if you have not reviewed the new commits. An explicit object ID states exactly which remote version you are willing to replace.

questions.title: A force-push removed commits from the server branch, but a coworker still has them. What should the team do?

options.text: Ask the coworker to create and push a new rescue branch at the old tip, then inspect and integrate it
Ask the coworker to force-push the old tip directly over the shared branch without checking current work
Have everyone delete and reclone before naming the old commit
Run `git reflog` in your clone and assume it contains the coworker's local branch history

questions.explanation: The coworker's clone may still contain commits that the server no longer names. They can push the old tip under a new rescue branch without changing the current shared branch. The team can then compare both histories and decide whether to cherry-pick, merge, or revert anything.
questions.references:
[Pro Git: About Version Control, distributed repositories](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Getting-Started-About-Version-Control)

[Pro Git: Working with Remotes](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Basics-Working-with-Remotes)

questions.title: After `git fetch` sees a force-update to `origin/main`, where might the old tip still appear?

options.text: The local reflog for `origin/main`, such as `origin/main@{1}`
A guaranteed server-side `HEAD@{1}` downloaded by fetch
The working tree's modification timestamps
The staging area under the old remote branch name

questions.explanation: `origin/main` is a local ref that fetch updates. Its reflog may still record the value from before the force-update, such as `origin/main@{1}`. This is local and temporary. It does not mean the server has a reflog you can read.
questions.references:
[Git manual: git-rebase, recovering from an upstream rebase](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rebase#_recovering_from_upstream_rebase)

[Pro Git: Remote Branches](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Remote-Branches)

questions.title: The reflog no longer names a lost commit, but the object may still exist. Which command can find dangling objects?

options.text: `git fsck --lost-found`
`git reset --hard --all`
`git reflog expire --expire=all --all`
`git clean -fdx`

questions.explanation: `git fsck` checks the object database and reports dangling objects. With `--lost-found`, Git writes dangling commits under `.git/lost-found/commit/` and other dangling objects under `.git/lost-found/other/`. It can only find objects that have not been pruned.

questions.title: By default, when do unreachable reflog entries become eligible for expiration?
questions.description: Assume `gc.reflogExpireUnreachable` has not been configured. Enter the number of days.
questions.explanation: `gc.reflogExpireUnreachable` defaults to 30 days. Ordinary reflog entries default to 90 days. Repository settings and explicit maintenance commands can change those periods. Expiring a reflog entry and pruning the object are separate events.

questions.title: Which facts explain why a reflog is not a backup system?

options.text: Reflogs are local and are not copied into every clone
Reflog entries expire according to maintenance policy
Once Git prunes an unreachable object, that repository can no longer recover it
A reflog makes every uncommitted editor buffer permanently recoverable

questions.explanation: A reflog is useful during recovery, but it is local and its entries expire. If no ref or reflog protects an object, maintenance may eventually prune it. Reflogs record ref values. They do not save uncommitted files or editor buffers. Keep important work in commits and maintain backups or other clones.
questions.references:
[Git manual: git-reflog](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-reflog)

[Git manual: git-gc](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-gc)

[Pro Git: Revision Selection, reflogs are local](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Tools-Revision-Selection)

questions.title: Can a reflog reliably recover unstaged edits erased by `git reset --hard`?

images.alt: A table comparing three git reset modes across three columns: HEAD (branch), Index (staged), and Working tree. `--soft` moves only HEAD, leaving the index and working tree unchanged. `--mixed`, the default, moves HEAD and resets the index but leaves the working tree unchanged. `--hard` moves HEAD, resets the index, and also resets the working tree, highlighted in red as the only mode that can discard uncommitted edits.
images.caption: `--hard` is the only mode that rewrites files on disk — the reflog records where refs pointed, not the file bytes it overwrote.

options.text: No. Reflogs record ref movement, not snapshots of unstaged files
Yes. `HEAD@{1}` always includes every byte from the old working tree
Yes. Git commits all unstaged edits automatically before a hard reset
No. A hard reset deletes the entire `.git` directory

questions.explanation: A hard reset makes tracked files match the target commit. A reflog only records where refs pointed. It does not contain ordinary unstaged content that Git never stored as an object. An editor's local history, a filesystem snapshot, or a backup may help, but Git does not promise recovery.

questions.title: You recovered one useful commit and want to add its change to the current branch. What should you use?

options.text: `git cherry-pick <recovered-commit>`
`git reset --hard <recovered-commit>`
`git reflog expire <recovered-commit>`
`git branch -D <recovered-commit>`

questions.explanation: Cherry-pick applies the recovered commit's change to the current branch and normally creates a new commit. Reset would move the branch itself and might also change the index and working tree. Give the recovered commit a rescue branch, inspect it, and then cherry-pick it.

questions.title: Three unpublished commits landed on `main`. How do you move them to a topic branch?
questions.description: The working tree is clean, nobody else has received these commits, and `main` should return to `HEAD~3`.

options.text: Create `topic/wip` at the current tip, reset local `main` to `HEAD~3`, then switch to `topic/wip`
Reset `main` first, expire the reflog, and hope the commits remain discoverable
Revert all three commits on `main` and then delete their objects
Force-push `main` before creating the topic branch

questions.explanation: Create `topic/wip` before the reset so all three commits have a branch name. Because the commits are unpublished and the working tree is clean, you can reset local `main` back three commits. Then switch to `topic/wip` and continue working. Resetting first would make recovery depend on the reflog.
questions.references: [Git manual: git-reset, moving commits to a topic branch](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-reset)

questions.title: A merge stopped at conflicts, and you want to abandon it. Which command should you run?

options.text: `git merge --abort`
`git rebase --skip`
`git revert MERGE_HEAD` before the merge has committed
`git branch -D HEAD`

questions.explanation: `git merge --abort` stops the merge and tries to restore the pre-merge state. Git may fail to reconstruct uncommitted changes if you modified them after starting the merge. Commit or stash important changes before merging when possible. An unfinished merge has no merge commit to revert.

questions.title: What is the safest order of work after a possible history-loss incident?

options.text: Stop making changes, inspect status and reflogs, create rescue refs, verify the commits, then choose the repair
Force-push immediately, then ask teammates which commits disappeared
Expire reflogs, run garbage collection, and start recovery after the repository is smaller
Run hard reset repeatedly until the working tree looks familiar

questions.explanation: Preserve evidence before moving more refs or changing files. `git status` shows uncommitted work. Reflogs and the commit graph help you find candidates, while rescue refs keep those commits reachable. Inspect the commits and diffs before choosing reset, revert, cherry-pick, or a coordinated rewrite. Repeated resets, garbage collection, and an early force-push can make recovery harder.
